source.title: Double Descent and Overfitting under Noisy Inputs and Distribution Shift for Linear Denoisers
source.authors: Chinmaya Kausik; Kashvi Srivastava; Rishi Sonthalia

record.tranche_reason: Tests double-descent and sample-size effects in noisy-input linear denoisers and regressors, rather than deep networks.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly reports double-descent curves and studies increasing training data through two augmentation procedures. Curves are shown without exact point values. Hyperparameter values used to select optimal training noise are not separate outcome rows; cited results from other studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study gives theory and experiments in a new setting: minimum-norm linear denoising and regression with noisy inputs, low-rank data and distribution shift. Test error is reported against c = d/N, with d fixed and N varied, so this is a sample-wise sweep. Results bear on V3, V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors derive instance-specific test-error formulas for low-rank, non-IID data that match real-data experiments within about 1% relative MSE. Test error shows double descent in c = d/N, peaking at c=1, even under distribution shift; they attribute this to input noise as an implicit regularizer that weakens near c=1. Optimal training noise does not remove the peak. Data augmentation lowers error for c<1 but raises it for c>1. Benign overfitting appears only in the limits of very small or very large c.
record.recipe_differences: Uses minimum-norm linear least squares with noisy inputs and data-dependent low-rank assumptions, rather than deep-network model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect of increasing sample count depends on which side of c = 1 the setting lies: the analysis predicts an increase toward the peak for c > 1 and a decrease farther from it for c < 1. The tested augmentation procedures and test distributions also differ.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal training-noise level itself follows a double-descent shape against c (Fig 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization-wise double descent: the optimal regularization strength peaks near the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Relative excess error tends to c/(1-c) or 1/(c-1), so overfitting is benign only as c→0 or c→∞.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign/tempered overfitting taxonomy for noisy-input linear models.

record.problems: The experimental claims are largely presented in plots without exact values or reported error bars. The theory assumes exactly low-rank data, and the experiments use a simple linear model; the paper notes that real data is only approximately low rank.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results left out.

untested.parts: All: no deep networks and no model-size sweep.
All: no single effective-complexity measure tested across axes.
Label-noise dependence; triple or multiple descent; optimally tuned explicit (ridge) regularization.
Model classes other than linear least squares; capacity sweeps other than the d/N ratio.

missing.what: Classification experiments: MSE double descent carries over to classification error for Gaussian clusters (Fig 3), but not always under transfer shift (Fig 4).
Mechanism: the variance term dominates, and the peak at c=1 comes from weakening implicit noise regularization and the large norm of Wopt.
missing.locator: Section 4, Double Descent under Distribution Shift; Theorem 1 scale discussion

record.verdict_notes: The sweep varies N with d fixed, so this is sample-wise double descent in a linear model; its link to V4 is by analogy to the overparameterization ratio. Several curves (Figs 5–6, theoretical curves in Fig 7d) are computed from the formula rather than from empirical runs. Belkin et al. (an original source) is cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: The reported evidence concerns noisy-input linear denoising/regression and particular data-augmentation settings, not a general sample-size result across model classes.
The tested class is minimum-norm linear denoising/regression; the paper does not test the curve across a range of other model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Tests optimizing the training-input-noise level, but not label-noise dependence, multiple or triple descent, or other forms of optimally tuned regularization.
No test of whether recounting complexity as an effective number of parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shape.
